content:
I'm co-leaning a formalization project with several goals:

  1. Make a (specific) contribution to Mathlib of something that is currently not there in an area of interest to us.

  2. Learn as much about Lean, the community, and formalization as possible!

This is for the Women in Topology workshop series so our team is already set. Everyone is new to formalization except me. Work is underway and should be completed within the year.

I feel like back in the day it was more common to discuss planned work here for student projects that didn't necessarily welcome contributors with the aim of making sure that someone else didn't inadvertently do the same thing in parallel. I'm wondering if we should try to relaunch this practice and if so am willing to offer this project as an experiment. (No one's thesis is at stake, so it's lower stakes than other possible experiments.)

I realize there are concerns now that someone can come along with AI and scoop the whole thing (and I suspect what we're aiming for is within the scope of AI). But we're trying to learn something so we're going to work (mostly? entirely?) AI free.

So the idea is to publicly declare our plans to work on X for Y period of time in the hopes that no one (human or AI) will work on the same thing in that period. And then we'll see if it works, if we can do our thing publicly and slowly, without someone else getting there first.

Would this be a valuable experiment for the community? If so, where should I announce our project? If not, what do you recommend otherwise?
That sounds like an excellent idea for an experiment, and I hope everyone in the community recognizes the value of projects of this nature.

I suggest a slight alteration towards shaping the community in the direction you want.

Rather than hope no one else is working on the same project, offer a controlled or limited exchange: Your group is interested in self-education currently, and (since the projects are public) anyone whose is interested in your area of study is welcome to observe.

If someone else is developing similar material in parallel, accept that fact and consider reviewing small pieces of their output, with the intention of determining what is good quality, what is educational, and other beneficial characteristics. Make yourself the point of contact so that any potential cross-fertilization (or contamination) is observed/directed/rejected by you or a designated project participant.

If the goal is to get Mathlib quality, I doubt there will be many who will try to "scoop" your efforts at getting Mathlib quality code in with AI. If the goal is to learn how to make Mathlib quality code, you might welcome some outside help if it is good.

I think if your topics of study are specific enough, you run little risk of someone providing better quality code before you are ready to provide it. This suggestion puts the spin of using the outside code as a teaching resource, where you decide if any part of it is appropriate for the group. You may even find a way to reframe this so that outside help is encouraged. Wouldn't that lead to (or at least suggest) a better notion of community?
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

content: We'd definitely be grateful for outside help. The one awkward thing, though, is that the Women in Topology group project format comes with the expectation that there will be a publication where the authors are the group members. So that's the motivation for limiting outside human involvement.

Hi @Emily Riehl ! This seems an excellent idea. We're discussing the points that you raise within the Maintainers team and we will provide some answer very soon about where to post this kind of messages and about our suggestions on how to move forward.

I haven't really thought through the details here, but I like the idea of some sort of "federated" system. Many individual projects have ways of claiming issues, but ideally we'd also have some global view of these intentions/claims.

I think it's really helpful if such "intention reports" also come with timelines (exactly as Emily is doing above!). It doesn't do the community any good when someone says "oh yes, I'm working on X, please don't work on it", and then a year passes and there's nothing to show for it. Credible timelines hopefully both engender more cooperative behaviour, and provide a simple mechanism for "releasing the claim".
Thanks. There's no particular rush. Please tag me with instructions whenever they're available.

I like the idea that there is a default mechanism where the claim is released at a particular time even if there is no further action/contact from the authors. And I was also imagining something weaker than a "claim" but more like a "courtesy" following usual practices within math research committees around known thesis projects.

Finally, I'm interested in this experiment from the setting of an autoformalizer too. Before starting an autoformalization project with a specific target that is missing from a HoTT library, we asked on the discord whether anyone is working on that result. But it would have been better if there was some public message board that could be used by everyone to find untargetted projects.
Let me know if there are further questions I can answer.
Thanks, I agree that this would make full sense and I also find it very interesting. We'll be back soon.

Note that a claim or notice of working on formalizing X does not automatically mean claiming or working on Y that X depends on. There's both "I'm working on X, at some point that will need Y and I'd be very happy if someone else does Y as long as they complete getting it into mathlib so I can use it" and "I'm working on X and, as part of that, its dependency Y".

Great idea @Emily Riehl I was thinking about similar things. HoTT was crowded when we started working on it, but at the same time we had a good community spirit. Are you proposing new mathematics, or "just" a new formalization. I'm curious whether you've thought about new math and formalization at the same time.

This doesn't address the headline question, but I just want to mention progress on the repository-level "intentions registration" front, which is that we've turn the existing issue claiming mechanism into a reusable github action, see #Project announcements > leanprover-community/intentions.

I hope that some standardisation here might help us later build federated systems that could register intentions across projects (and perhaps even across closed projects, starting to address Emily's request).
This has now converged, and more details can be found here: thanks @Emily Riehl for motivating us to work on this!
